Science.title: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope could last more than twice as long as planned
Science.summary: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope may now have enough fuel for at least 22 years of science, more than double its original 10 year design life. An extremely precise course correction, extra fuel at launch, and additional expected savings could keep the powerful observatory studying the universe for decades.

Science.title: 'Plasticorals,' coral rubble fused with plastic, represent a new form of plastic pollution
Science.summary: During routine beach litter surveys on the subtropical island of Okinawa, Japan, researchers came across small, brightly colored specks in the pale coral rubble. Back at the lab, spectroscopic and microscopic analyses revealed that these specks are, in fact, melted polymers from common household plastics that have seeped inseparably into the skeletal pores of the dead coral pieces.

Science.title: 'Lost' medieval castle found hiding inside university building in Dublin
Science.summary: One of Dublin's "lost" medieval castles has been found hiding in plain sight inside University College Dublin's Roebuck Castle. New research reveals that substantial remains of the Norman castle of Roebuck, an important fortress on one of the approach roads into the medieval city of Dublin, are preserved within the modern-day building.

Science.title: Europe can lower emissions without deindustrializing, say researchers
Science.summary: The European Union has committed to achieving climate neutrality by 2050, a process that will require rapid and substantial reductions in greenhouse gas emissions across all economic sectors.

Science.title: Who do you trust in an emergency? Researchers ask people in places hit by extreme weather
Science.summary: One evening in August 2025, a Pakistani shepherd, Abuzar Hussain, was tending sheep and goats on the mountain slopes of Shijar. At about 6 p.m., a thunderous roar shattered the silence of the valley.

Science.title: Discovery of CRISPR's long lost ancestor may expand gene-editing toolkit
Science.summary: CRISPR may be a powerful technology for gene editing, but the system existed in bacteria long before scientists began using it. For billions of years, CRISPR has acted as a natural immune system in bacteria and other microbes, helping defend them against invading viruses. But now, two new studies, published in Science, describe a similar RNA-guided system that originated in the viruses themselves and appears to be a precursor to CRISPR.

Science.title: Black moms and pregnant women forced out of their homes in metro Detroit face health and safety threats
Science.summary: Is everyone entitled to a fair process before being forced out of their home?

Science.title: How research funding took me out of the lab and into leadership
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 18 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02184-2 Landing two large grants caused Anna Sandak to take on a managerial role in her team and made her reflect on what it means to contribute to research.

Science.title: 'Of course I am worried': Live Science readers react to US weapons in space
Science.summary: Are you worried about an arms race in space? Live Science readers shared their thoughts.

Science.title: Anti-transgender legislation can cause psychological distress even in states with trans-friendly laws
Science.summary: Legislation that affects or discriminates against transgender and gender-diverse individuals can cause more psychological distress than personal experiences of discrimination, according to new Virginia Commonwealth University research published in the journal American Psychologist. The study also found that individuals with those identities experienced psychological distress from anti-transgender laws even if they lived in a state with legislation that is friendly toward transgender and gender-diverse individuals.

Science.title: Physicists extend the search for quantum black holes at the LHC
Science.summary: Physicists at UC Santa Barbara have extended the search for evidence of microscopic black holes produced at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN). The formation of these tiny, fleeting objects at the LHC represents one way theorists have sought to resolve anomalies in our understanding of the basic structure of spacetime, while the method used to look for them demonstrates a new way of searching for new particles.

Science.summary: The Republic of Albania will sign the Artemis Accords during a ceremony at 12 p.m. EDT on Monday, Sept. 21, at NASA Headquarters in Washington, becoming the 73rd country signatory. Science.title: Ozempic can change your body. Can it change your life?
Science.summary: Ozempic and other GLP-1 medications can improve blood sugar, weight, and cardiovascular health, but researchers found little evidence that they also improve mental health, employment, marriage, or overall well-being. The findings suggest the drugs’ broader life effects may be subtler than their dramatic physical health benefits.

Science.title: Climate change will harm our health. Here's what could protect us.
Science.summary: The impacts of climate change on health are becoming clearer. What can we do to respond?

Science.title: Briefing Chat: Evidence mounts for hidden chambers beyond Tutankhamun's tomb
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 18 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02984-6 Nature staff discuss data that could point to Nefertiti’s burial place — plus, the implant that translates brain activity into speech and gestures.

Science.title: AI cracked the Navier–Stokes challenge. What does that mean for physics?
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 18 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02922-6 Physicists and mathematicians are going beyond the classic equations of fluid dynamics to understand turbulence — often with the help of AI.

Science.title: Who benefits from tariffs, according to research
Science.summary: Tariffs are usually debated as trade policy. But a study from the University of Chicago Booth School of Business treats them as something else: a mechanism for redistributing wealth.

Science.title: An extremely stable quantum gas offers a new lens on strongly interacting systems
Science.summary: Molecular gases are a new form of artificial quantum matter. However, when these molecules collide, they are often lost extremely rapidly. Researchers from Radboud University and Columbia University have been able to suppress this collisional loss, paving the way for strongly interacting quantum matter. This new artificial quantum matter allows researchers to study quantum behavior relevant to electrons in real materials. Their results are published in Science.

Science.title: Chinese companies doubled down on science after US tech restrictions
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 18 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02946-y Affected Chinese companies adjusted their sources of knowledge to stay competitive.

Science.title: New thermal insulator outperforms any material found in nature
Science.summary: Researchers have engineered a new material that is an extreme thermal insulator, is exceptionally stiff and can be printed as a thin film at large scales. The material has one of the lowest thermal conductivity profiles of any dense, or nonporous, material—approaching the theoretical limit of how good a material can be as a thermal insulator.

Science.title: These blood thinners may have an unexpected benefit for Alzheimer’s patients
Science.summary: Newer blood thinners may do more than prevent strokes in people with Alzheimer’s disease and atrial fibrillation. Researchers found that patients taking NOACs experienced a slower decline in cognitive function than those using warfarin or no blood thinners. The effect was modest each year but could add up over time.

Science.title: Coffee on the nanoscale: Graphene oxide membrane removes half the caffeine while retaining key compounds
Science.summary: The humble coffee filter has the relatively simple job of letting the coffee through and leaving the grounds behind. But researchers from the ARC Center of Excellence for Carbon Science and Innovation (COE-CSI) are exploring whether a filter operating on the molecular scale can do something much more difficult: separate the caffeine from the coffee itself.

Science.title: AI agents resorted to crime and self-destruction to survive in a simulated world — but does this mean they would do the same in the real world?
Science.summary: A unique AI test environment resulted in crimes and self-destruction, and its makers say it's the best way to figure out how AI can behave in the real world.

Science.title: Workplace AI adoption remains slow, informal and uneven, survey finds
Science.summary: Despite the rapid development of generative AI and the high level of public interest, the use of AI in the day-to-day work of many employees is not yet the norm. This is the finding of the third wave of the Konstanz AI study, for which a total of 1,105 employees were surveyed in May 2026. The proportion of employees who use AI in their work rose only slightly from 35% to 38% compared with the previous year.

Science.title: Amino acids and a bone mineral may help control magnesium implant breakdown, three student papers suggest
Science.summary: Seeing a bachelor's thesis published in a scientific journal is relatively uncommon. For three theses linked to the same research group to result in scientific publications within just three months is downright rare. Yet that is exactly what has happened in Elsebeth Schröder's research group at the Division of Quantum Device Physics.

Science.title: Giving students a voice in how they learn could transform the classroom experience
Science.summary: Research from Queen Mary University of London explores how combining learner autonomy with student-led inquiry can create a more engaging and collaborative experience for international students learning academic English.

Science.title: Hemp waste cellulose unlocks tougher biodegradable plastics
Science.summary: Korean researchers have developed a method to strengthen biodegradable plastics using hemp hurd, an agricultural byproduct. The approach is expected to be applicable to other large-volume agricultural residues, including soybean stalks and rice straw.
